title: Why Languages Disappear
paras: Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, but nearly half of them may disappear before the end of this century. Many have fewer than a thousand speakers, and a large number are used only by elderly people. When the last fluent speaker of a language dies, an entire way of describing the world disappears with them, often without anyone outside the community noticing. Most of the languages at risk are found in remote mountain areas, islands and forests, where small groups have lived apart for centuries.

Languages rarely vanish because they are banned; far more often they fade through gradual pressure. When a community moves from villages to cities, parents discover that jobs, schools and government services all use a dominant language. They begin to speak it at home so that their children will succeed, and within two or three generations the young people understand the old language but no longer speak it. Linguists call this process language shift.

Economic forces are therefore powerful, but history also matters. Colonial administrations and national education systems have often punished pupils for using local languages in the classroom, teaching them that these languages were backward. Such attitudes leave lasting shame, and some families still hesitate to pass on their mother tongue. Modern media add to the pressure, since films, websites and software are produced mainly in a small number of widely spoken languages.

Why does this matter? A language stores knowledge built up over centuries, including the names of local plants, methods of farming and stories about the landscape. Some communities have words for weather patterns that scientists have only recently begun to study. Linguists also value endangered languages because their grammar can challenge assumptions about how human language works. For the speakers themselves, the language is a central part of their identity and sense of belonging.

Reviving a language is difficult, but it has succeeded in some places. Successful programmes tend to share several features: young children are taught in the language at nursery school, older speakers are paid to teach, and the community itself decides the goals. In several regions, so-called language nests, in which elders look after small children and speak only the heritage language, have produced a new generation of fluent speakers within about ten years. Such results are encouraging, because they show that a language with very few speakers can still recover when the next generation is given the chance to learn it.

Technology can help as well as harm. Speakers now record dictionaries on smartphones, publish stories online and use messaging apps to write in their own language. Researchers are also building speech-recognition tools for languages that have little written material. Yet experts agree that no recording can replace daily use. A language survives only when people choose to speak it with their children.

title: Storing Renewable Energy
paras: Solar panels produce electricity only when the sun shines, and wind turbines only when the wind blows. Demand for power, however, rises and falls according to the habits of people: it is often highest in the early evening, when homes are lit and cooked in but the sun has already set. Unless surplus energy can be stored and released later, electricity from renewable sources cannot fully replace power stations that burn fuel on demand.

The oldest and most widespread solution is pumped hydropower. When there is more electricity than needed, water is pumped uphill into a reservoir; when demand rises, the water is released through turbines and generates power again. The method is reliable and can supply a city for many hours. Its weakness is geography, because it requires suitable mountains and large amounts of water, and building a new reservoir can damage local ecosystems.

Batteries are the best-known alternative. Lithium-ion batteries, the type found in phones and electric cars, are now installed in large containers next to solar farms. They respond within fractions of a second, so they are excellent for stabilising the grid. Yet they usually store energy for only a few hours, and mining the metals needed to make them raises environmental and social concerns. Researchers are therefore testing cheaper designs that use more common materials, such as sodium or iron.

Another approach is to store energy as heat. In one design, surplus electricity heats a tank of molten salt or a pile of hot rock, and the heat is later used to boil water and drive a turbine. The materials are cheap and last for decades. Heat storage is particularly attractive for factories, which need high temperatures anyway, and for district heating networks that supply hot water to entire neighbourhoods.

Hydrogen offers a way to store energy for weeks or even months. Electricity splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, the hydrogen is kept in tanks or underground caverns, and it can later be burnt or used in a fuel cell. The disadvantage is inefficiency: a large share of the original energy is lost during the process, so hydrogen is expensive. Specialists therefore expect it to be used mainly for industries that are hard to electrify, such as steel production and shipping.

No single technology will solve the problem. Most experts expect future power systems to combine several kinds of storage, together with smarter ways of managing demand. For example, electric cars can be charged when electricity is plentiful and cheap, and washing machines or water heaters can be programmed to run at the same times. Better storage will not make renewable energy free, but it will make it dependable enough to power daily life. The challenge is now less about invention than about building enough capacity quickly and at a reasonable price.

title: The Psychology of Decision-Making
paras: We like to believe that our choices are the result of careful reasoning, yet psychologists have shown that many decisions are made quickly and almost automatically. Researchers often describe two systems of thinking. One is fast, intuitive and effortless; the other is slow, deliberate and tiring. In everyday life we rely on the fast system for most things, from choosing a sandwich to judging whether a stranger looks friendly, and we call on the slow system only when a problem seems difficult or important.

The fast system uses mental shortcuts, known as heuristics. They are usually helpful, because they save time and energy, but they can also lead to predictable mistakes. One example is the availability heuristic: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind. After reading several news reports about an aeroplane accident, many people feel that flying is dangerous, even though statistics show that it is among the safest forms of travel.

Another well-documented pattern is anchoring. When people are given a number before they make an estimate, that number influences their answer, even if it is clearly irrelevant. In one type of experiment, volunteers who first saw a high random number guessed higher prices for ordinary objects than those who saw a low one. Sellers use the same effect when they display a high original price beside a reduced one, making the discount appear generous.

Emotion also shapes decisions. People generally dislike losses more than they enjoy equal gains, a tendency called loss aversion. As a result, an investor may keep a falling share for too long, hoping to avoid admitting a loss, and a shopper may buy an unnecessary extra item because it is presented as a last chance. Tiredness and hunger make matters worse; studies suggest that decisions made late in a long day are more likely to be cautious or careless.

Understanding these tendencies does not remove them, but it allows people and organisations to design better choices. Some governments, for instance, enrol workers automatically in pension schemes, while still allowing them to leave. Because most people accept the default option, participation rises sharply without anyone being forced. Hospitals use checklists for similar reasons: a simple list prevents experienced doctors from forgetting steps when they are under pressure.

Individuals can also improve their own decisions. Waiting a day before a major purchase, asking someone with no stake in the outcome for advice, and writing down reasons for and against an option all give the slow system time to work. Psychologists do not claim that people should analyse every choice; that would be exhausting and impractical. The aim is to recognise the few situations where a little extra thought is worth the effort.
